chapter: Publishing, Jelly Roll in Los Angeles and band lore
title: Leek's Lake and the Wayside Park dance hall in Watts
summary: Reacting to Mister Jelly Roll, Spikes says he built the Watts dance hall facing Leek's Lake around 1922 and sold it to Jelly Roll's band for $800 after rheumatism struck.

story.theme_name: Dance halls, lake camps and riverboat bandstands
story.community_name: Dance halls, lake resorts and where bands played

blocks.x: In the book Mr. Jelly Roll by Alan Lomax--have you seen this book?
No.
Well, uh, let me show you.
Got a lot of stuff here...only thing he want to talk about is Jelly Roll, so I guess that was how it was.
How long ago was that?
I don't remember.

You're in a footnote here. He's talkin' about Anita, and "Anita decided to stay in Los Angeles. She bought a small hotel on the corner of Central near Twelfth and named it 'The Anita.' By that time, I had several little businesses [Jelly Roll talking] branching out myself. I had a little dancehall but because you had to

close the dance hall at twelve o'clock, I went partners with Pops Woodward, the trombone player, and we opened up The Wayside Park at..."

That was the place I built...out in Watts. See, I called it Leek's Lake at first because it was uh...this guy had a ...next door, had a little old lake there where he raised bullfrogs to sell then, and I bought four, five lots along here, and I put my dance-hall over here and I called Leek's Lake. His name was Leek's Lake. His name was Leek but he had a great big place there...oh, big...bigger'n' this house...it...an' a little lake that he raised bullfrogs. So my dancehall was facin' this lake. Then afterwards, you see, where it says that on there that...uh, uh, Kid Ory 'n' them played out at...what'd they call it there? Wayside Park?
Wayside Park.
Yeah, well, that's my place.
You said Watts Country Club. Is that another...

Well, I said...was in Watts. When I first opened it, I called... And when I uh...uh...when I sold it, I sold it to Jelly Roll and the band. There were about ten or twelve of 'em, and I sold it, I think, for eight hundred dollars, so they give me about eighty dollars or somethin' apiece. It cost me about three thousand to build it but I had made my money, and I got sick. I was sick about five years because out there at night, you see, it was during the bootleggin' days, and my sister--I had her on the door selling tickets and things, and I'd walk around outside in the fog and uh...until the dance closed and after they closed, watchin' the bootleggers...'cause it was out in the country,

SPIKES - 153
Reel 5

and they...all the bootleggers was out there sellin' their booze, and I'd run them off of there, and I got...I used to come in at nights--that fog would have me all wet down to here, see, and I got down in the bed, and I was down 'bout a year and a half with...just stiff as a board with rheumatism, so I sold it out to the...the uh...the boys, and they ran it--the band ran it.
I see. Oh, it says, quoting Jelly Roll, "We opened up the Wayside Park at Leek's Lake out in Watts County..."
That's right. I told you Leek's Lake.

"...There we could stay open all night. Wayside Park is the place King Oliver made much fame in later when I introduced him there in April, 1922." Is that right? Jelly Roll presented King Oliver there in 1922?
No, because I...I...I I don't think it's '22. I...I...I didn't build it till '22--'21 or '22. '22, I think, when I built it, and I ran it a coupla years. Must have been '24 or '25.
Then there's a foot note, and it says: "Reb Spikes says, 'I built up Leek's Lake out in Watts--made a pile of money, too. They call it Wayside Park today but it's still Leek's Lake to me.'"
[Laughs] Yeah, I built it. I built it from the ground up.
Is that all you found in there about me?
Yeah, that's all I found in there but there's some other things about Los Angeles, which, maybe they got part of it from you. There's no index in this book, and I read this book a long
